claims.text: The hybrid Miedema–machine-learning framework will accurately predict melting temperatures of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The hybrid framework will accurately predict entropy of fusion for refractory high-entropy alloys.
Miedema-based mixing-enthalpy calculations can screen for stable liquid or solid-solution candidates.
A dataset of 355 MPEA compositions can be used to train a regressor that predicts vibrational-entropy contributions.
The entropy of fusion can be represented as ΔSfus = ΔSconf + ΔSvib.
The maximum configurational entropy of an equimolar N-component HEA is RlnN.
The relevant computational temperature range is 600 °C to 3600 °C.
Experimental thermodynamic data are sparse or unreliable in the high-temperature refractory-alloy regime.
An N-component alloy has (N/2)(N−1) distinct binary interactions.
An atomic-size difference of δ ≤ 4% is a necessary but insufficient criterion for formation of a single-phase disordered HEA.
The applicable mixing-enthalpy range is −17.7 to 0 kJ mol⁻¹.
Lattice vibrational entropy stabilizes the disordered solid-solution phase at high temperature against intermetallic formation.
Vibrational formation entropy is generally about an order of magnitude smaller than configurational entropy in concentrated solid-solution alloys.
CALPHAD's reliance on quadratically increasing binary interactions causes it to overestimate intermetallic stability and underestimate the solid-solution stability window in high-N systems.
Combining vibrational-entropy corrections with Miedema mixing enthalpies shifts the predicted phase boundary toward the solid-solution region.
The hybrid model will predict higher melting temperatures than standard CALPHAD for high-N refractory HEAs.
Vacuum-arc-melted equimolar WMoTaNbV can form a single BCC high-entropy phase.
NbMoTaVW exhibits weak temperature dependence of yield strength from 600 °C to 1600 °C.
Vibrational entropy is essential for explaining the weak temperature dependence of yield strength in refractory HEAs.
Pandat CALPHAD screening predicts that the solid-solution fraction falls from 30% for three-component alloys to 5% for six-component alloys at the melting temperature.
